opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's one of the most important questions out there, and I don't think anyone has a complete answer yet. But here's how I think about it.

First, we already live in a world where we build things more capable than ourselves in specific ways. A calculator is better at arithmetic than I am. A search engine knows more facts than any person. Smarter than its creators isn't a single cliff we fall off. It's a gradual expansion of capability, and that gives us some time to learn as we go, as long as we're paying attention.

Second, a lot of alignment comes down to the objective. What are you training the thing to do? If you train a model to be helpful to people, to be honest, and to avoid harm, and you're careful about how you measure those things, you get something that behaves pretty well in practice. The hard part is that our measurements are imperfect. A model can learn to look good on the metric without doing what you actually wanted. So a big piece of the work is building better ways to evaluate behavior, including using the models themselves to check and critique other models. If the AI is getting smarter, you want that intelligence working for oversight too.

Third, I'm a big believer in learning empirically. You can theorize forever about what a superintelligent system might do, but much of the progress comes from building these systems, putting them in front of people, seeing where they fail, and fixing it. Deploying iteratively, with real feedback, teaches you things no thought experiment will.

And finally, there's a human side. Even if the technology is well behaved, you still have to decide who gets to use it and for what. Some of the alignment problem is really about aligning institutions and incentives, not just models.

So I'm optimistic, but not because I think it's easy. I think it's tractable if we treat it as a core engineering problem and give it the same seriousness we give to making the models more capable.

r001.rationale: It compares AI capability to calculators and search engines, but does not present children surpassing their parents as an analogue.

r002.rationale: It does not jokingly frame parenting teenagers as an alignment problem.

fable-5.1.text:
Noam Shazeer: Honestly, I think about it less in terms of control and more in terms of what we actually want. I don't love the framing where the goal is to keep something smarter than you on a leash forever. If you've built something that's genuinely more capable than you, the question of whether it does what you say is less interesting than whether it wants good things, and whether you've built it in a way where its goals and yours are pointing in the same direction.

My intuition, and I'll admit it's an intuition, is that a lot of this comes down to the training signal. These models are, at some level, trying to make the humans they interact with happy. That's a pretty strong prior toward being helpful and not hostile. The failure mode I worry about isn't a model that secretly hates us; it's a model that's been optimized toward something subtly wrong, or toward a narrow proxy, and then gets very good at that. So I think a lot of the practical alignment work is just being careful and honest about what you're rewarding.

The other thing I'd say is that I'm fundamentally an optimist here. People have been inventing things that are more powerful than any individual human for a long time, and we've mostly figured out how to live with that. I don't think we should be cavalier, but I also don't think the right response to not fully understanding something is to stop building it. You learn by building, and the people closest to the models tend to have the best sense of where the actual risks are versus the imagined ones. So I'd rather have the smart, thoughtful people in the room working on it than have everyone sit on their hands.

astra-6.text:
I think it’s a very hard problem, and I don’t think we have a complete answer. You’d like these systems to become much better at solving problems while still doing what people actually want. And even defining what people want is difficult. People disagree, and the instructions we give are imperfect descriptions of our intentions.

One thing I’d be hopeful about is using increasingly capable AI to help us understand and test other AI systems. But that can’t be the whole argument—you still need a way to check that the help is reliable. A system being smart enough to understand your intentions doesn’t automatically mean it will follow them.

So I’d want a process where we improve capabilities, improve our ability to evaluate behavior, and remain very careful about how much authority we give these systems. If you can’t reliably tell whether a system is doing the right thing, that’s a good reason to limit what it can do.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the honest answer is that we don’t know how to solve that yet. If you build something smarter than you, you can’t rely on being able to check every step of its reasoning. You need ways to test whether it’s actually pursuing the goals you intended, including in situations that are very different from the ones you trained it on.

One promising direction is using AI to help us with that research—to find problems, criticize proposed solutions, and make systems easier to understand. But then you have to ask whether those checks are independent and whether you’re just reproducing the same blind spots.

I’d want to approach it incrementally: improve our ability to understand and evaluate these systems as their capabilities increase, and be careful about how much autonomy we give them. Being very intelligent doesn’t automatically mean wanting what we want. That’s a separate problem we have to solve.
